title: PH-MissBench: Rare-Outcome Prediction Tasks with Real, Agency-Documented Missingness from U.S. Birth Records
content: Background. Missing-data methods are usually compared on complete datasets with values deleted by simulation, which ﬁxes the missingness mechanism by design. How methods behave on the missingness that public health analysts actually face is less well studied, particularly for rare outcomes. Methods. PH-MissBench is an open benchmark built from U.S. National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) natality public-use ﬁles for 2022–2024. Every predictor cell carries the missingness class documented by NCHS (observed, not stated, structurally not applicable, or imputed by NCHS), and NCHS-imputed values are restored to missing. Two tasks predict early preterm birth (obstetric-estimate gestation under 34 weeks) and very low birthweight (under 1,500 g) among singleton births to U.S. residents from 35 pre-pregnancy and prenatal items, with training on 2022–2023 and testing on 2024. Task ﬁles were hashed and frozen before any baseline was run. Six baselines were evaluated by area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) with 1,000-replicate stratiﬁed bootstrap intervals. Results. The cohort comprised 6,324,305 training, 703,612 validation and 3,512,264 test births; test-year prevalence was 2.15% for early preterm birth and 1.06% for very low birthweight. The pipeline reproduced NCHS published birth totals exactly for all three years. In 2024, 38.23% of births had at least one predictor missing. Gradient boosting with native missing-value handling performed best (AUPRC 0.082 and 0.050); mean imputation with missing-value indicators (0.067, 0.038) outperformed chained-equations (0.063, 0.035) and iterative random-forest imputation (0.064, 0.036); complete-case analysis performed worst (0.061, 0.034) and was miscalibrated. Conclusions. On population-scale U.S. birth records, approaches that let the model see missingness outperformed imputation alone, consistent with informative missingness. PH-MissBench provides frozen, reproducible tasks for comparing missing-data methods on real public health data.
